the concept of "missing mass" emerged from attempts to reconcile astronomical observations with Newtonian dynamics. It was demonstrated that if galactic rotation curves are non-Keplerian, their flat profiles imply the presence of additional mass extending well beyond a galaxy's visible edges. In 1997, Famaey and Gentile introduced a semi-heuristic approach to derive a quantitative lower bound on this missing mass under the assumption of flat rotation curves. Today, with high-resolution gas and star formation data enabling detailed mappings of mass distributions across various components of starburst galaxies, it is both necessary and feasible to update this derivation to explicitly incorporate the actual observed mass distributions of these systems. Applying this revised method to the ULIRG IC\.1459, our results indicate that the missing mass constitutes 2.6 times the visible mass and has a lower bound of 1.5 times the galaxy's total baryonic content. Furthermore, we find that this missing mass follows a flat profile and shares the same morphology, extent, and kinematics as the visible components, strongly suggesting that it is distributed cold dark matter (CDM). These findings support the long-standing hypothesis that the significant baryonic concentrations observed in IC\.1459 and similar ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs) have been accreted from larger volumes of space already dominated by CDM. Finally, we emphasize that precise measurements of rotation curves in gas-rich systems remain essential for directly detecting the anticipated peaks in the density profiles of this missing mass, which should align with the characteristic scales of the predicted NFW or other standard CDM profiles.
